strengths: Introduces a novel construction of vector diffusion wavelets for geometric graphs with vector-valued node features, combining vector diffusion maps/local coordinate frames with geometric scattering. This fills a gap in prior geometric scattering work, which largely handled scalar signals or manifold discretizations without vector features.

Provides theoretical results, including frame bounds for the vector diffusion wavelet transform (Theorem 3.1) and equivariance of the wavelets and scattering coefficients under rotations (Theorems 3.2 and 3.3), with detailed proofs in the appendix. The frame-bound proof is a reasonable reduction to scalar diffusion wavelets via a unitary change of variables.

The architecture is well motivated and described: scalar and vector tracks, within-track mixing, invariant feature extraction, and task-specific heads are clearly specified. Complexity analysis and runtime tables are included, and the experiments demonstrate the practical benefit of equivariance on rotated synthetic point clouds.

Empirical results are promising on the synthetic tasks: ESc-GNN maintains performance on rotated test sets while non-equivariant baselines degrade sharply, and it achieves comparable or better MSE than EGNN and TFN with far fewer parameters (e.g., 59,779 parameters versus 284,036 for EGNN and 29,672,961 for TFN in the graph-level task).
The paper includes an ablation (non-equivariant ESc-GNN) that helps isolate the effect of equivariance, and the synthetic tasks are designed so that rotation equivariance is directly relevant.
weaknesses: The central SE(3)-equivariance claim is overclaimed relative to the theory. The theorems establish SO(d) rotational equivariance only; translation equivariance is neither proved nor tested. For absolute coordinate vector features, the vector diffusion operator Q applied to translated positions is generally not a translated output, so the method is not obviously SE(3)-equivariant in the usual sense. The experiments rotate but never translate the data, leaving the SE(3) claim unsupported.

The sign-ambiguity handling in Appendix C is not rigorous. The proposed inner-product sign-flipping does not guarantee a globally consistent choice of local frames on graphs with cycles; for a cycle, sign propagation can be frustrated, so O_{i,j} may not satisfy the relation used in Proposition B.3. Since Proposition B.3 is the basis for Lemma A.3 and Theorems 3.2/3.3, the equivariance proof has a significant gap. A determinant-based gauge fix (e.g., enforcing det(U_i)=+1) would address this for SO(d), but is absent. The assumption of distinct singular values is also not justified.

The experimental validation is narrow: only synthetic 3D point clouds sampled from ellipsoids. No real molecular or geometric graph benchmarks (e.g., QM9, MD17, OC20) are used, so the claimed applicability to molecular graphs is not demonstrated. The parameter-efficiency comparison is also somewhat inflated by comparing against a very large TFN configuration (ℓ=2, ~30M parameters) without including more parameter-efficient equivariant baselines such as e3nn-based models.

Reproducibility is weakened by a missing code URL (the appendix says the code is 'available at' with no link) and by ambiguous implementation details around the sign-flipping procedure. The reference list contains multiple errors (e.g., 'Singer and Thomsen' for Singer and Wu, 'Wenkel et al. 2020' for Thomas et al., inconsistent Tong et al. citations), and there are several presentation typos.

The theory does not directly cover the actual implemented model: the experiments use InfoGain-selected generalized wavelets, omit nonlinearities inside the scattering transform, and add Dirac scalar features. The paper asserts that the guarantees 'may be readily adapted' but provides no proof or formal statement for this modified setting. The limitations of the method—scalability, sign ambiguity, translation, and real-world applicability—are not discussed in a limitations section.

strengths: Provides a coherent and reasonably novel construction: combining vector diffusion maps / connection-Laplacian style parallel transport (local frames via SVD of neighbor offsets) with geometric scattering to obtain an equivariant transform that handles vector-valued node features, which prior geometric-scattering works did not.

The theoretical results are mostly correct and clean. Lemma A.2 (Q^m[i,j] = P^m[i,j] O_{i,j}), the frame-bound Theorem 3.1, and the equivariance Theorems 3.2/3.3 are proved with understandable arguments, and the underlying parallel-transport composability (O_{i,k}O_{k,j}=O_{i,j}) is a nice structural property.

Strong empirical parameter efficiency: ESc-GNN (57k-60k params) matches or beats EGNN (284k-835k) and TFN (~30M) on both tasks, and the ablation (ESc-GNN non-equivariant) and the rotated-test-set protocol make a convincing case that the equivariance property is the source of the generalization benefit.

Good reproducibility practices: code link, detailed architecture, complexity analysis, runtime tables, full hyperparameter listings, and 5-fold cross-validation with honest reporting of high-variance baselines.
The paper is generally well organized and the exposition of the scalar scattering background and the equivariant-GNN setting is clear.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to synthetic point clouds sampled from random ellipsoids. There are no real-world benchmarks (e.g., QM9, MD17, OC20), so the central claim of 'comparable performance to other equivariant GNNs at a fraction of the parameter count' is only demonstrated on toy tasks that are essentially engineered to showcase equivariance. For an ICML main-track contribution framed as a practical alternative to equivariant MPNNs, this is an important evidential gap.

The abstract claims SE(3)-equivariance (rigid-body roto-translations), but only SO(d) rotational equivariance is proved or tested. Translation equivariance/invariance is never addressed, so the headline claim overstates what the theory supports.

Theorem 3.3 requires the activation to commute with rotations; standard activations (ReLU, tanh) do not. In the experiments the authors explicitly remove the nonlinearity from the scattering coefficients ('we did not use a non-linearity while computing the scattering-coefficients'), so the model reduces to a (linear) diffusion/wavelet mixing plus MLPs. This undercuts the 'scattering transform' premise and renders the equivariance theorem partly vacuous for the actual model used.

The sign-flip convention (Appendix C) is not rigorously justified. The claim that flipping u_{j,l} whenever <u_{i,k},u_{j,l}> < 0 yields a globally well-defined O_{i,j} is hand-wavy, since row/column flips cannot make all entries of a general orthogonal-frame product non-negative and per-edge flip decisions may conflict across multiple neighbors. The paper also assumes distinct singular values (and implicitly that every node has at least d neighbors) without discussing these genericity assumptions or their failure modes.

The frame-bound constant c*d_min/d_max can be extremely small (large degree spread), so the claim that the transform 'may be stably inverted and is robust to noise' is a weak guarantee that is not quantified or tested.

Baseline comparisons are not apples-to-apples: TFN is configured at ~30M parameters (a strawman in practice), and no modern equivariant architectures (e.g., SEGNN, higher-order e3nn models, MACE-style) are included. Parameter-count comparisons against a grossly over-parameterized TFN do not strongly support the efficiency claim.
No limitations discussion: the synthetic-only scope, the genericity assumptions (distinct singular values, minimum degree), and the linear-scattering caveat are not acknowledged.

strengths: Introduces a novel vector diffusion wavelet construction using local coordinate frames and connection Laplacian for equivariant scattering on geometric graphs with scalar and vector node features.
Provides theoretical results: frame bounds for the vector wavelets and equivariance to SO(d) rotations for the wavelets and scattering coefficients.
Demonstrates on synthetic tasks that the equivariant ESc-GNN achieves competitive performance with far fewer parameters than baselines like EGNN and TFN.
Clearly shows the benefit of equivariance: non-equivariant models fail on rotated test sets while equivariant ones do not.
Includes a detailed computational complexity analysis and thorough experimental setup, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The sign-flipping technique in Appendix C is mathematically flawed/ambiguous: it claims to make all inner products nonnegative by flipping individual columns, which is impossible for general orthogonal matrices; this may break the cocycle condition O_{i,k}O_{k,j}=O_{i,j} required for Q^m and equivariance. The equivariance proof assumes \overline{U}_i = R U_i, but it is unclear that the described sign-flipping guarantees this.
Experiments are only on synthetic 3D point clouds (ellipsoids) and do not include real-world molecular or geometric datasets, limiting evidence for practical utility and significance.

The efficiency claim is not fully supported by parameter-matched comparisons; baselines like EGNN and TFN are much larger but not tuned to similar parameter counts, so 'comparable performance with fraction of parameters' is not a controlled comparison.
The abstract claims SE(3)-equivariance (roto-translations), but the theory only covers SO(d) rotations; translation equivariance/invariance is not formally addressed.
The paper lacks a limitations discussion and does not discuss failure cases, scalability, or the impact of sign ambiguity on practice.
There are several typos and citation errors (e.g., 'singal', 'Gaussian', misattribution of Singer and Wu, wrong LEGS reference), and the code URL is missing.

strengths: Introduces vector diffusion wavelets (VDWs) for graphs with vector-valued node features, extending diffusion wavelets via vector diffusion maps and the connection Laplacian.
Provides theoretical results including frame bounds and rotational equivariance, with proofs and a clear connection to scalar diffusion wavelet theory.

Demonstrates effectiveness on three diverse tasks: synthetic ellipsoids, wind field reconstruction, and neural activity representation learning, with competitive performance and improved parameter efficiency.
Well-motivated and clearly positioned relative to prior work on diffusion wavelets, geometric scattering, and equivariant GNNs.
Includes detailed experimental setups, complexity analysis, and reproducibility information (e.g., hyperparameters, hardware, cross-validation).
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are relatively straightforward corollaries of scalar diffusion wavelet results, relying on unitary similarity to P ⊗ I; technical novelty is limited.

The sign-flipping procedure in Appendix C is mathematically problematic: it is generally impossible to make all pairwise inner products between two orthonormal frames nonnegative unless the frames are permutation-equivalent. As described, this may not produce a consistent set of local frames, potentially undermining the cocycle property O_{i,k}O_{k,j}=O_{i,j} used in Lemma A.2 and the frame bound proof.

The equivariance claim is not consistently demonstrated: the wind-field VDW-GNN concatenates raw 3D coordinates into an MLP, breaking rotational equivariance, yet the paper reports rotated MSE and compares to equivariant baselines. The neural experiment also uses an MLP on vector coefficients, which is likely not equivariant. This disconnect between theory and implementation weakens the claimed benefits of equivariance.

Empirical gains are modest: on wind field reconstruction, VDW-GNN is within noise of EGNN and GCN; on neural data, the improvement over MARBLE is not statistically significant. The large outperformance of DD-TNN may be due to an unfair comparison (e.g., directed graph construction not supported by DD-TNN).
No dedicated limitations section; some presentation issues (notation errors, missing code availability statement) and reliance on a single dataset per real-world task.

strengths: Introduces a novel extension of diffusion wavelets to vector-valued signals by leveraging vector diffusion maps and the connection Laplacian, with a concrete construction of a vector diffusion matrix Q.
Provides theoretical results (frame bounds and rotational equivariance) with proofs in the appendices, attempting to place the method on firm mathematical ground.

Demonstrates the approach on three diverse domains (synthetic ellipsoids, wind field reconstruction, neural activity) and reports computational efficiency (fewer parameters, faster per-epoch training) compared to baselines.
The architecture is lightweight and uses sparse matrix operations, avoiding explicit eigendecompositions, which could aid scalability.
Includes detailed experimental hyperparameters and model configurations in the appendices, aiding some reproducibility.
weaknesses: Fundamental flaw in the local frame construction: The sign-flipping trick in Appendix C claims to make O_{i,j}=U_i U_j^T well-defined by ensuring all inner products <u_{i,k},u_{j,l}> are nonnegative, but this is impossible in general. For a generic rotation between two local frames, no sign choices can make all entries of an orthogonal matrix nonnegative. Consequently, the claimed well-definedness of O_{i,j} fails, and the proofs of Lemma A.2, Theorem 3.1 (frame bounds), and Theorem 3.2 (equivariance) rely on an invalid assumption.

The theoretical frame bound theorem assumes an undirected connected graph, but the wind field experiment uses directed edges (observed -> masked) and an out-degree matrix for P. The theoretical guarantees therefore do not apply to this experiment, yet the paper presents it as a validation of the method.

The neural activity comparison is unfair: VDW-GNN is trained with a supervised contrastive loss that uses condition labels, while the baselines (MARBLE, CEBRA, LFADS) are described as unsupervised. The reported 66% vs 65% accuracy is not statistically significant (Wilcoxon p-value not significant), so the claim of outperforming MARBLE is unsupported.

The 'inductive' evaluation in the neural experiment is not truly inductive: test-trial embeddings are computed via a neighbor-based distillation using training-set neighbors rather than a forward pass of the learned model. This is closer to transductive/out-of-sample extension and may not probe generalization as claimed.

Empirical gains on real-world tasks are marginal: on wind field reconstruction, VDW-GNN's MSE (2.7546) is essentially tied with EGNN (2.7651) and GCN (2.8662), with no statistical significance testing. On synthetic node-level tasks, TFN outperforms VDW-GNN. The experiments do not isolate the benefit of vector diffusion wavelets over scalar diffusion wavelets applied coordinate-wise with an equivariant architecture.

Reproducibility and presentation issues: No code or repository link is provided. The reference list contains numerous errors (e.g., 'AMSI' appears in place of author names, wrong years for Chew et al. and Defferrard et al., inconsistent citations). There are typos and formatting glitches (e.g., 'VDW-GNN' inserted in text, index errors in theorem statements).

The theoretical results are largely reductions to the scalar diffusion wavelet case (Q' = P ⊗ I) via a change of variables, so the novelty of the frame bound proof is limited. The equivariance proof assumes the local frames rotate exactly as \overline{U}_i = R U_i, which is not guaranteed by the proposed sign-flipping algorithm.
Limitations are not adequately discussed: the sign ambiguity, directed graph setting, supervised loss in neural experiments, and potential sensitivity to implementation choices are not addressed.

strengths: Introduces a novel and natural extension of diffusion wavelets to vector-valued signals using vector diffusion maps and the connection Laplacian, enabling geometric GNNs on tangent-bundle data.
Provides theoretical results on frame bounds and SO(D) rotational equivariance, which if correct would give useful guarantees for vector-valued wavelet transforms.

Synthetic ellipsoid experiments convincingly demonstrate the importance of rotational equivariance: non-equivariant models fail on rotated test sets, while VDW-GNN is robust and achieves strong performance with far fewer parameters than EGNN and TFN.

Real-world experiments on wind field reconstruction and neural activity data show competitive or best performance with lightweight models, and the neural experiment uses a more stringent inductive evaluation protocol than prior transductive work.
The method is computationally efficient: Q is sparse and cached, and the appendix provides detailed complexity analysis, hyperparameters, and implementation notes that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem 3.1 (frame bounds) appears flawed. The key equality (8) does not hold in general; a simple counterexample with n=2, D=2 shows ||\tilde W_J y||^2 ≠ ||\tilde W_J w||^2. The proof actually bounds a different operator (e.g., \tilde W'_J w or \tilde W_J y), not \tilde W_J w, so the central frame-bound claim is not established as written.

The SVD sign-flipping procedure is mathematically inconsistent. Enforcing all inner products <u_i,k, u_j,l> ≥ 0 is generally impossible for nontrivial rotations, and per-edge sign flips break the cocycle property O_{i,k} O_{k,j} = O_{i,j} required in Lemma A.2 and the equivariance proofs. No globally consistent synchronization algorithm is provided.

The neural experiment compares VDW-GNN trained with a supervised contrastive loss (using condition labels) against MARBLE, which uses an unsupervised contrastive loss. This gives VDW-GNN an unfair advantage and confounds the comparison.

The wind experiment reports a rotated test MSE (3.2266) noticeably higher than the unrotated MSE (2.7546) for VDW-GNN, which contradicts exact rotational equivariance. EGNN reports identical rotated/unrotated MSE, which may indicate a copying error or that rotations were not properly applied.
No code or anonymized repository is provided, limiting reproducibility despite detailed appendix descriptions. The critical sign-flipping implementation is not fully specified.
The assumption that all singular values have multiplicity one is strong and unaddressed for real data; robustness to noise, deformation, or repeated singular values is not theoretically analyzed.
Minor citation error: LEGS is cited as Tong et al. (2020) but the method likely refers to Tong et al. (2024). There is also no limitations section discussing failure modes or broader impact.
